extracted.intended_audience: literate London/Westminster reading public (coffee-house readers) — general readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical moral and social essays (The Spectator) offering prescriptive observations and advice on manners, truth, marriage, superstition, club behaviour, and public decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biter / Biting (wit that deceives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Biter' is defined as "one who thinks you a Fool, because you do not think him a Knave." 'Biting' is a way of wit grounded in deceit: making another believe something serio-usly and then triumphing in having deceived them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt or admire 'biting' wit that depends on deceiving the unsuspecting. The essay condemns sharpers and fashionable fops who use 'Bite' to evade serious discourse or to mask nonsense as jest. Examples and anti-patterns: sharpers likened to foxes preying on lambs; a wit who cries 'Bite' to dismiss a serious admission in debate; the anecdote of the rogue who takes a surgeon's guinea and then cries 'Bite, I am to be hang'd in Chains.' The surrounding commentary urges readers to reject this frivolous, pernicious custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-interpretation and other divination (superstition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay treats the many arts of prediction—palmistry, physiognomy, astrology, augury, interpreting entrails, and especially dream-interpretation—as groundless, uncertain, and chimerical; dreams are commonly misvalued by the vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Root out popular errors and do not place weight on dreams or trivial signs. The text satirizes a would-be 'Oneirocritick' advertising interpretation services (charging different rates, offering to interpret from a single circumstance or water), illustrating how such trades comfort the curious and prey on credulity. Footnote/context: Moorfields and Bedlam as locales associated with prophets and conjurers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving love after marriage: neatness, discretion, and active esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Love in marriage is endangered by too great familiarity, neglect of decency (especially in dress), and the abandonment of efforts to please; similarity of humours alone does not ensure affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To keep love alive: maintain neatness and common rules of decency; continue an earnest endeavour to please on both sides; cultivate good sense (learning) in the man; retain some engagement in business to provide occasion for absence and to display talents; give genuine compliments and open new conversational worlds to one's partner. Examples: Lætitia and Erastus (complaisance, improving her self-regard) versus Flavilla and Tom Tawdry (vain dress, neglect, and contempt). Anti-pattern: assuming the 'bait' is unnecessary after marriage and thus abandoning the arts of pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness vs. party-lying (condemnation of factional falsehoods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Party-lying—propagating systematic falsehoods in service of political faction—is a dominant vice. Though common, it remains morally culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject justifications for party-lying: (1) numbers do not diminish individual guilt — spreading a lie does not divide the guilt but multiplies it for each actor; (2) loss of shame among a multitude does not erase the moral wrong; (3) 'doing good to a cause' cannot morally justify falsehoods. Practical admonition: be on guard in coffee-houses and the press where factional stories are routine; maintain duty to truth even when tempted by party advantage (quoting Plutarch/Pompey and moral exemplars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to tyrannical conduct in clubs (proper club governance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Club rulers who assume arbitrary, uncontroulable authority (exemplified by 'Dionysius' the proveditor) are likened to tyrants: they impose edicts about what to eat, where to go, interrupt or force conversation, and exert petty despotism over fellow members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members should recognize and resist such tyranny. Practical responses include forming a conspiracy to dethrone the usurper or otherwise undermining his power (the essay suggests patient counsel and ultimately decisive action). The description details the tyrant's tactics (changing taverns, commanding attendance, issuing non-negotiable orders) to help readers identify the vice and plan redress; Milton quoted to show seriousness of remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility toward women in mixed company (conversational conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentlemen should not treat women as if they were men indifferent to gentleness; rude contradiction and insulting suppositions are improper treatment of a female guest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat women with the gentle respect due to sisters or mistresses rather than with the brusque contradictions of a fop. Avoid making offensive suppositions, public contradiction, or behaviour that effectively 'banishes' a female guest from agreeable company. The letter requests maxims of behaviour and suggests public reprimand may reform offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thrift and public decorum (signs of a thriving frugal man; proper use of the Royal-Exchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thriving, frugal man's character shows in regularity across expense, dress, servants, and house. Public spaces like the Royal-Exchange ought to reflect commercial dignity and be kept for honourable merchants and tradesmen rather than overrun by beggars and vulgar vendors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restore simplicity of manners and public order as indicators of civic and commercial prosperity. The essay laments the Exchange being crowded by 'mumpers, the halt, the blind,' and petty vendors (e.g., walnut sellers leaving shells and trash), arguing that if men of consequence cease to frequent such places, civic commerce and decorum decline. The implied prescription: preserve public spaces for their proper commercial uses and maintain private regularity as a mark of thrift.
